slides.label: 03 Accounting and finance
slides.html:
BUS311 · Corporate Finance

Accounting
and Finance

How financial statements become cash-flow evidence for valuation and decisions

Professor Bethany Evitts · Endicott College · Gerrish School of Business
slides.note: Introduce the distinction between accounting performance and the cash available for financial decisions.

slides.label: 04 Three pillars of corporate finance
slides.html:
The management job

Corporate finance balances three connected decisions

Orientation
slides.note: Connect investing, financing and working-capital choices to the financial statements students will use.

slides.label: 05 Key financial statements
slides.html:
The evidence base

Three statements answer three different questions

Financial statements
Snapshot

Balance sheet

What does the firm own, and what does it owe, at one point in time?

Assets = Liabilities + Equity

Performance

Income statement

How much profit did the firm generate over a period?

Revenue − Expenses = Income

Movement

Cash flow statement

Where did cash come from, and where did it go?

Operating + Investing + Financing

Common-size statements turn dollars into percentages so firms of different sizes can be compared.
slides.note: Ask which statement answers a question about profit, resources or cash over a period.

slides.label: 06 The balance sheet
slides.html:
Statement 1

The balance sheet is a point-in-time snapshot

Balance sheet

It reports the resources the company controls, the claims creditors hold, and the residual interest belonging to shareholders.

Assets = Liabilities + Equity

Finance uses this statement to assess liquidity, capital structure, and the resources available to generate future returns.
slides.note: Emphasize that the balance sheet is a snapshot at a date, unlike period flows.

slides.label: 07 Mind the GAAP
slides.html:
Comparability

GAAP makes the comparison rules visible

Balance sheet

Generally Accepted Accounting Principles govern how U.S. companies prepare, present, and report financial information.

01

Consistency

Similar transactions are classified and measured using shared conventions.

02

Comparability

Analysts can make a more credible apples-to-apples comparison.
slides.note: Explain that accounting measurement requires conventions; book value is not automatically market value.

slides.label: 08 Common-size financial statements
slides.html:
Standardize before comparing

Common-size statements reveal structure, not scale

Analysis
Balance sheet

Percent of total assets

Shows how the firm allocates resources and finances those resources.

Income statement

Percent of sales

Shows margins and the cost structure behind each revenue dollar.

Cash flow statement

Percent of sources or uses

Shows which activities create or consume cash.
slides.note: A common-size denominator makes firms and periods comparable. Check what each percentage divides by.

slides.label: 09 Common-size walk-through
slides.html:
FactSet walk-through

Convert each balance-sheet line into a share of total assets

Analysis
Line item ÷ Total assets × 100%

The percentage answers a cleaner question: “How much of the asset base sits in this account?”

Compare with care

Use the same fiscal period, accounting basis, and currency before interpreting differences.
slides.note: Ask students to interpret a percentage change in composition before judging it as good or bad.

slides.label: 10 Assets liabilities and equity
slides.html:
The balance-sheet architecture

Resources sit on one side; claims sit on the other

Balance sheet
slides.note: Have students distinguish resources from the claims that finance them.

slides.label: 11 Key balance-sheet equation
slides.html:
The balancing relationship

Equity is what remains after every liability is paid

Equity = Assets − Liabilities
slides.note: The balance-sheet identity must hold. A balanced model can still contain offsetting mistakes.

slides.label: 12 Homeowner balance sheet
slides.html:
Personal analogy

A home makes the balance-sheet equation tangible

Balance sheet
Asset
$700K

Home value

Liability
$560K

Mortgage

$700K − $560K = $140K equity

The homeowner’s equity is the residual claim—not the full value of the house.
slides.note: Use the home analogy to distinguish an asset value from the owner’s residual equity.

slides.label: 13 Short term versus long term
slides.html:
Classification

Timing separates current accounts from long-term accounts

Balance sheet
Assets

Current

Expected to become cash, be sold, or be used within one year.

Cash · Receivables · Inventory

Assets

Long term

Support operations and growth beyond the next year.

Property · Equipment · Intangibles

Liabilities

Current

Must be settled within one year.

Payables · Accrued expenses · Short-term debt

Liabilities

Long term

Come due after one year.

Bonds · Bank loans · Lease obligations
slides.note: Classify items by maturity, then connect the classification to liquidity.

slides.label: 14 Net working capital
slides.html:
Short-term financial health

Net working capital measures the liquidity cushion

Balance sheet
Current assets
−
Current liabilities
=
NWC

Positive NWC can support day-to-day operations—but too much may signal cash tied up in inventory or receivables.
slides.note: General NWC is current assets minus current liabilities. The Coastal cash-flow model uses operating NWC, excluding cash and interest-bearing debt.

slides.label: 15 Debt versus equity
slides.html:
Funding the firm

Debt promises repayment; equity shares ownership

Capital structure
Debt financing

Borrow capital

Interest and principal create contractual claims. Debt can be cheaper, but it increases financial risk.

Lender return = interest + principal
Equity financing

Exchange ownership

No required repayment, but new owners share control and future upside.

Owner return = dividends + price gain

Most firms use both. The decision is about cost, flexibility, control, and risk.
slides.note: Debt creates contractual claims; equity bears the residual risk and reward.

slides.label: 16 The income statement
slides.html:
Statement 2

The income statement explains profitability over time

Income statement

Revenue shows what the company earned. Expenses show what it consumed to earn that revenue. The residual is profit.

Revenue − Expenses = Income

Unlike the balance sheet, the income statement covers a period: a month, quarter, or year.
slides.note: The income statement measures performance over a period, not cash in the bank.

slides.label: 17 Income statement math
slides.html:
The simplest version

The top line funds every cost before it becomes the bottom line

Revenue
Top line
−
Expenses
=
Income
Bottom line
slides.note: Build operating profit before financing costs and taxes. Keep D&A separate from cash operating expenses.

slides.label: 18 Per-share metrics
slides.html:
Translate totals into ownership units

Per-share metrics connect company results to one share

Income statement
EPS

Earnings per share

Net income ÷ Shares outstanding

How much profit is attributable to each common share?

DPS

Dividends per share

Total dividends ÷ Shares outstanding

How much cash distribution is paid for each share?
slides.note: Check share counts, time periods and units when interpreting per-share measures.

slides.label: 19 Taxes
slides.html:
A profit is not fully available to investors

Taxes change the cash that remains

Finance distinguishes the rate paid on total income from the rate applied to the next dollar earned.
slides.note: Explain why taxes affect cash available to investors.

slides.label: 20 Marginal versus effective tax rates
slides.html:
Tax vocabulary

Marginal and effective rates answer different questions

Taxes
Marginal tax rate

The next dollar

The statutory rate applied to an additional dollar of taxable income.

Useful for forecasting how an incremental decision changes taxes.

Effective tax rate

The total result

Total tax expense divided by pretax income.

Useful for understanding the overall tax burden reported by the company.
slides.note: Distinguish an incremental tax rate from taxes divided by pretax earnings.

slides.label: 21 Average versus marginal tax rate
slides.html:
The denominator matters

The average rate uses all income; the marginal rate uses the last dollar

Taxes
Average rate = Total tax ÷ Total income
Marginal rate = Tax on the next dollar

Decision rule

For a new project, use the marginal rate because the project creates incremental taxable income.
slides.note: Have students state which tax rate fits the question being asked.

slides.label: 22 Depreciation amortization and cash flow
slides.html:
Accounting expense, cash-flow adjustment

Depreciation and amortization

They reduce accounting income without using cash in the current period.
slides.note: Noncash expenses reduce accounting profit but do not require a contemporaneous payment.

slides.label: 23 Depreciation versus amortization
slides.html:
Match the expense to the asset

Both allocate cost over time—but for different assets

Cash flow
Tangible assets

Depreciation

Spreads the cost of physical assets such as equipment, buildings, and vehicles across their useful lives.

Non-cash expense → add back
Intangible assets

Amortization

Spreads the cost of patents, trademarks, and other finite-lived intangibles across their useful lives.

Non-cash expense → add back
slides.note: Distinguish allocation of tangible and intangible asset costs from the timing of cash spending.

slides.label: 24 The cash flow statement
slides.html:
Statement 3

The cash flow statement tracks money moving through the firm

Cash flow

Accrual accounting explains performance. Cash flow explains liquidity and the funds available to creditors and shareholders.

Cash flow from assets = Cash flow to creditors + Cash flow to stockholders
slides.note: The accounting cash-flow statement reports operating, investing and financing flows. The cash-flow-to-investors identity is a separate analytical view.

slides.label: 25 The illusion versus the reality
slides.html:
Case: the bakery

A profitable business can still run out of cash

Cash flow
slides.note: Ask why reported profit can diverge from cash collected and spent.

slides.label: 26 Profit is an opinion cash is a fact
slides.html:
The finance lens

“Profit is an opinion. Cash is a fact.”

Net income contains estimates and accruals. Cash flow focuses on money the firm can spend, reinvest, or return.
slides.note: Use the quotation as a prompt to trace cash rather than assume earnings are cash.

slides.label: 27 Free cash flow analogy
slides.html:
The personal analogy

Free cash flow is the firm’s discretionary income

Free cash flow
slides.note: Discuss the limits of the household analogy: firms must reinvest and meet capital-provider claims.

slides.label: 28 Defining free cash flow
slides.html:
Cash flow from assets

Free cash flow is the surplus available to all capital providers

The firm has already covered operations, taxes, and the reinvestment required to sustain the business.

FCF = Operating cash flow − Net capital spending − Change in NWC
slides.note: This textbook cash-flow-from-assets convention uses OCF before the working-capital deduction. The later FCFF bridge explicitly removes financing-related tax effects.

slides.label: 29 Operating cash flow
slides.html:
Component 1

Operating cash flow isolates cash generated by the business

Free cash flow
Textbook OCF = EBIT + D&A − Taxes

D&A is added back because it reduced accounting income without using cash in the current period.

2024 U.S. Corporation$
EBIT694
Add: Depreciation65
Less: Taxes(131)
Operating cash flow628
slides.note: Textbook OCF here equals EBIT plus D&A minus actual taxes. It excludes an interest deduction and precedes the NWC deduction. Do not substitute statement CFO.

slides.label: 30 Operating cash flow bridge
slides.html:
From accounting to cash

Start with operating earnings, reverse non-cash expense, then pay taxes

Free cash flow
EBIT
+
D&A
−
Taxes
=
OCF

Textbook OCF comes before the NWC deduction. Statement CFO starts with net income and includes the working-capital adjustment.
slides.note: Actual taxes can include an interest tax shield. Later NOPAT applies the tax rate to EBIT to obtain an unlevered measure.

slides.label: 31 Reinvestment requirements
slides.html:
Components 2 and 3

Growth consumes cash through fixed assets and working capital

Free cash flow
Fixed assets

Net capital spending

Cash invested in property, plant, equipment, and other long-lived operating assets.

Operating assets

Change in NWC

Cash tied up—or released—through inventory, receivables, payables, and other current accounts.

Reinvestment = Net capital spending + Change in NWC
slides.note: Reinvestment has both long-lived-asset and operating-working-capital components.

slides.label: 32 Investing for growth
slides.html:
You have to spend money to make money

Reinvestment moves cash out today to support cash in tomorrow

Free cash flow
slides.note: Ask students to predict the direction of cash effects before computing them.

slides.label: 33 Capital spending
slides.html:
Net capital spending

CapEx measures the cash committed to long-lived assets

Free cash flow
Ending fixed assets − Beginning fixed assets + Depreciation

Depreciation is added because the ending balance is shown after accounting depreciation.

2024 U.S. Corporation$
Ending fixed assets1,709
Less: Beginning fixed assets(1,644)
Add: Depreciation65
Net capital spending130
slides.note: CapEx is a cash use; D&A is an allocation of prior asset cost. The simple PP&E bridge assumes no disposals or other adjustments.

slides.label: 34 Cost of growth
slides.html:
Reinvestment drags

Growth can reduce current free cash flow for good reasons

Free cash flow
CapEx

Build capacity

New equipment, facilities, and technology consume cash now but may expand future operating cash flow.

ΔNWC

Fund the operating cycle

More sales can require more inventory and receivables before the related cash is collected.

Negative free cash flow is a signal to investigate—not an automatic verdict.
slides.note: Negative free cash flow warrants investigation of investment quality and funding capacity.

slides.label: 35 Change in net working capital
slides.html:
Working capital over time

The change in NWC measures cash tied up between periods

Free cash flow
ΔNWC = Ending NWC − Beginning NWC

Interpret the sign

Increase in NWC: cash outflow.

Decrease in NWC: cash inflow.
slides.note: An increase in operating NWC absorbs cash; a decrease releases cash. Distinguish the balance from its change.

slides.label: 36 Change in net working capital calculation
slides.html:
Calculation

Working capital rose by $391, so $391 of cash was reinvested

Free cash flow
Ending NWC − Beginning NWC

A positive change reduces free cash flow because more cash is tied up in current operating assets.

2024 U.S. Corporation$
Ending NWC1,075
Less: Beginning NWC(684)
Change in NWC391
slides.note: Require a consistent beginning and ending definition before subtracting NWC balances.

slides.label: 37 Master formula
slides.html:
The master formula

Operations create cash; reinvestment claims part of it

Free cash flow = OCF − Net capital spending − ΔNWC
slides.note: Build cash flow from assets from textbook OCF, net capital spending and the change in NWC. Keep definitions consistent.

slides.label: 38 Cash flow from assets
slides.html:
Put all three components together

The firm generated $107 of free cash flow

Free cash flow
2024 U.S. Corporation$
Operating cash flow628
Less: Net capital spending(130)
Less: Change in NWC(391)
Cash flow from assets107
Interpretation
$107

Cash remained for creditors and stockholders after operations and reinvestment.
slides.note: Use the numeric example to distinguish gross operating cash generation from cash remaining after reinvestment.

slides.label: 39 Free cash flow waterfall
slides.html:
Follow the cash

Strong operating cash flow can be absorbed by reinvestment

Free cash flow
slides.note: Trace operating cash generation through both reinvestment deductions to the residual.

slides.label: 01 Caterpillar financial analysis
slides.html:
Applied finance warm-up

Caterpillar financial analysis

Read the business behind the statements, then explain what changed.
slides.note: Introduce the separate CAT research activity. It is an application of real-company data, not a required input to Coastal.

slides.label: 02 CAT analysis instructions
slides.html:
In class or homework

Build a year-end view of Caterpillar

Applied finance
1

Open the separate CAT FactSet activity workbook.

2

Use FactSet to fill the requested financial, cash-flow, and stock data in the green cells.

3

Calculate percentage changes in the blue cells, then submit the completed file in Canvas.

Separate application: record year-end periods and units; submit the completed CAT file and interpretations as assigned.
slides.note: Use the CAT workbook separately, in class or as assigned homework. Record fiscal year, units and field definitions before interpreting trends.

slides.label: 40 What to do with cash flow
slides.html:
Capital allocation

What should the firm do with its cash?

The answer should depend on value creation—not simply on whether cash is available.
slides.note: Ask students what additional evidence they need before deciding whether to distribute cash.

slides.label: 41 Where does the cash go
slides.html:
The distributable surplus

Free cash flow belongs to creditors and stockholders

Capital providers
slides.note: This is the textbook distribution identity. Later FCFE measures capacity, not necessarily cash actually paid to owners.

slides.label: 42 Cash flow to creditors
slides.html:
Debt holders

Creditors receive interest, net of new borrowing

Capital providers
Cash flow to creditors = Interest paid − Net new borrowing

Issuing new debt brings cash into the firm, so it reduces the net cash paid to creditors.

2024 U.S. Corporation$
Interest paid70
Less: Net new borrowing(46)
Cash flow to creditors24
slides.note: New borrowing offsets cash paid to creditors because it is a cash source to the firm.

slides.label: 43 Cash flow to stockholders
slides.html:
Owners

Stockholders receive distributions, net of new equity raised

Capital providers
Cash flow to stockholders = Dividends paid − Net new equity raised

Selling new shares brings cash into the firm, so it offsets the cash paid out to existing owners.

2024 U.S. Corporation$
Dividends paid123
Less: Net new equity(40)
Cash flow to stockholders83
slides.note: Distinguish distributions from net equity issuance. Cash available and cash distributed need not be equal.

slides.label: 44 Free cash flow heartbeat
slides.html:
The heartbeat of the firm

Profit is an opinion. Cash is a fact. Free cash flow is the heartbeat of the firm.
slides.note: Ask students to restate the profit-to-cash distinction in their own words.

slides.label: 45 Accounting to valuation
slides.html:
The bridge

Statements describe the past; cash flow connects that history to value

Valuation
slides.note: Financial statements supply historical evidence; valuation requires forward-looking cash flows and risk assumptions.

slides.label: Cash-flow definitions
slides.html:
Keep the definitions consistent

Textbook OCF and statement CFO are different starting points

Textbook OCF

EBIT + D&A − taxes

Before the working-capital deduction. Used in the earlier cash-flow-from-assets example.

Statement CFO

Net income + D&A − Δ operating NWC

Includes interest through net income and the working-capital adjustment.

Coastal uses CFO. Operating NWC excludes cash and interest-bearing debt.
slides.note: Explain why subtracting the change in NWC from CFO again would double-count it. In the simplified case, FCFF = CFO + after-tax interest − CapEx. Textbook cash flow from assets using actual taxes need not equal tax-unlevered FCFF.

slides.label: 46 FCFF from cash flow from operations
slides.html:
Route 1: start with CFO

Unlever operating cash flow before valuing the entire firm

FCFF
FCFF = CFO + Interest × (1 − t) − CapEx

U.S. GAAP classifies interest paid in operating cash flow. Adding back after-tax interest removes the financing choice.

Why unlever?

Value operations first

FCFF is available to debt and equity holders, so the cash flow should be independent of how the business is financed.

Discount FCFF at WACC.
slides.note: Under the simplified US GAAP case, CFO already includes interest and working-capital effects. Add back after-tax interest for FCFF; do not subtract NWC twice.

slides.label: 47 Deriving FCFF from EBIT
slides.html:
Route 2: start with EBIT

The operating engine builds FCFF directly

FCFF
EBIT × (1−t)
NOPAT
+
D&A
−
CapEx
−
ΔNWC
=
FCFF

NOPAT measures after-tax operating profit before financing; D&A is added back because it is non-cash.
slides.note: NOPAT is EBIT after operating taxes. Add back D&A, then deduct CapEx and the increase in operating NWC.

slides.label: 48 Who gets the cash
slides.html:
The great bifurcation

Firm cash flow and equity cash flow value different claims

FCFF vs. FCFE
slides.note: Have students identify the capital providers entitled to each cash-flow measure.

slides.label: 49 Whole pie versus slice
slides.html:
Two perspectives

FCFF values the whole business; FCFE values the owners’ slice

FCFF vs. FCFE
Unlevered perspective

The whole house

Looks at cash generated by operations before debt claims.

Metric: Enterprise value
Levered perspective

The homeowner’s equity

Looks at cash remaining after the mortgage and other debt effects.

Metric: Equity value
slides.note: Use the property analogy to distinguish enterprise value from equity value.

slides.label: 50 Levered free cash flow
slides.html:
Value the owners’ claim

FCFE is the cash available after servicing debt

FCFE
FCFE = FCFF − After-tax interest + Net borrowing
Perspective

Shareholders

Residual owners of the business.

Use case

Payout capacity

Dividends and share repurchases.

Discount rate

Cost of equity

Match the risk of the equity claim.
slides.note: FCFE is a capacity measure after debt effects, not a record of dividends paid.

slides.label: 51 Shareholder residual
slides.html:
From firm value to equity value

New borrowing is a current cash inflow to shareholders

FCFE
FCFE = FCFF − Interest × (1−t) + Net borrowing
FCFE = CFO − CapEx + Net borrowing
The counter-intuitive lever

Borrowing adds cash today

Net borrowing equals new debt issued minus debt repaid. It increases current FCFE, but it also creates future obligations.

Cash inflow today is not free value.
slides.note: New borrowing adds current cash and future obligations; it does not create operating profit.

slides.label: 52 Give it a try
slides.html:
Live you try it

Calculate FCFF, then FCFE

Practice
Revenue
$100M
EBIT
$20M
D&A
$5M
Tax rate
25%
CapEx
$6M
ΔNWC
$2M
Interest
$2M
Net borrowing
$0

Work in pairs for 2 minutes. Write both formulas, calculate FCFF and FCFE, and identify who can claim each flow.
slides.note: Allow two minutes in pairs. Students write both equations before substitution and compare the claims represented.

slides.label: 53 Give it a try solution
slides.html:
Solution

The business generates $12M for the firm and $10.5M for equity

Practice
FCFF · Unlevered

Build from EBIT

20 × (1−25%) + 5 − 6 − 2
$12.0M
FCFE · Levered

Remove after-tax interest

12 − 2 × (1−25%) + 0
$10.5M
slides.note: Formative answer: FCFF is 12.0 and FCFE is 10.5 million. The difference is after-tax interest of 1.5; net borrowing is zero.

slides.label: 54 Strategic decisions based on cash flow
slides.html:
From measurement to management

Do firms make strategic decisions based on cash flow?

Yes—but the decision depends on when cash arrives, how risky it is, and what alternatives are available.
slides.note: Move from measurement to a decision, asking what risks could change the conclusion.

slides.label: 55 Connecting FCF to decision making
slides.html:
Capital budgeting

Invest when the present value of future FCF exceeds the cost

Decision making
PV of future FCF
−
Investment cost
=
NPV
NPV > 0

Invest

The project is expected to create value.

NPV < 0

Reject

The project is expected to destroy value.
slides.note: Positive NPV means value exceeds investment cost under the assumptions; cash availability alone is insufficient.

slides.label: 56 Using FCF for decision making
slides.html:
Capital allocation choices

Positive free cash flow creates options—not an automatic payout

Decision making
slides.note: Compare reinvestment, payouts and debt repayment using value creation and financial flexibility.

slides.label: 57 Connecting cash flow to valuation
slides.html:
Discounted cash flow

Value is the present value of cash the asset can generate

Valuation
Value = Σ FCFt ÷ (1 + r)t

Forecast cash flow, choose the rate that matches its risk, then discount each future amount to today.

g

Growth

Changes in long-run growth can move value materially.

r

Discount rate

More risk raises the required return and reduces present value.
slides.note: Introduce the future cash-flow, growth and discount-rate inputs without requiring a full valuation model in M03.

slides.label: 58 Fundamental theorem of finance
slides.html:
The fundamental theorem of finance

“The value of any asset is the present value of its future cash flows.”
slides.note: Restate value as discounted future cash flows; match the risk and recipient of those flows.

slides.label: 59 Corporate finance cheat sheet
slides.html:
Match cash flow to discount rate

Use the firm lens or the equity lens—then stay consistent

Cheat sheet
FCFF · Unlevered
EBIT(1−t) + D&A − ΔNWC − CapEx

Discount at WACC

Produces enterprise value.

FCFE · Levered
FCFF − Interest(1−t) + Net borrowing

Discount at cost of equity

Produces equity value.

Golden rule: never discount FCFE at WACC.
slides.note: Ask students to match FCFF with WACC and enterprise value, and FCFE with cost of equity and equity value.

slides.label: Coastal guided practice
slides.html:
Partner activity · 20 minutes

Trace Coastal’s profit into cash available to investors

Profit → CFO → FCFF → FCFE

Open the starter workbook

Complete yellow cells on Cash Flow. Routine links are supplied; check each section as you finish.

Explain the bridges

Why does working capital use cash? Why does borrowing affect FCFE?

Deliverable: completed Cash Flow tab and a working-capital explanation.
slides.note: Allow 20 minutes in pairs. Use the separate private activity key to debrief the Coastal outputs. Do not require the optional balance-sheet extension before discussing cash flow.

slides.label: Coastal payout decision
slides.html:
Partner decision · 10 minutes

Calculate a payout ceiling, then recommend an amount

Maximum extra payout = MAX(0, cash − reserve)

Cash generated this year

FCFE is a period flow. Account for dividends and repurchases already made.

Cash available today

Ending cash includes beginning cash and prior distributions. Preserve the required reserve.

Complete Decision Memo: recommend an amount, cite three numbers, and name a monitoring trigger.
slides.note: Allow 10 minutes. Distinguish the mechanical maximum from the recommended payout. Require students to explain FCFE versus cash on hand and match each cash flow with its discount rate. Use the private key for case-specific answers.

slides.label: 60 Reading the signals
slides.html:
Interpretation and nuance

Negative FCF means “investigate,” not always “avoid”

Interpretation

SBC caution: stock-based compensation is non-cash today but dilutes owners. Treat an automatic add-back with care.
slides.note: Negative FCF is a prompt to investigate growth spending, operating weakness and financing runway.

slides.label: Coastal inventory experiment
slides.html:
Predict and test · 5 minutes

More inventory can turn positive free cash flow negative

Inputs!C17: 170 → 230

Before changing the input

Predict the effect on profit, CFO, FCFF, FCFE and cash.

After changing the input

Record the results. Explain whether the inventory supports growth or signals slow sales.

Record your explanation in Decision Memo, then restore inventory to 170.
slides.note: Allow five minutes in pairs. The isolated inventory increase leaves profit unchanged and reduces CFO, FCFF, FCFE and ending cash by the additional investment. Discuss inventory quality and funding capacity. Use the private key for exact case outputs.

slides.label: 61 Key takeaways
slides.html:
Key takeaways

Accounting tells the story; cash flow tells us what the story may be worth

Synthesis
01

Statements

Start with comparable, well-understood accounting data.

02

Cash

Add back non-cash expense and subtract reinvestment.

03

Perspective

FCFF values the firm; FCFE values equity.

04

Consistency

Match the cash flow to its discount rate.
slides.note: Use the four takeaways to connect accounting inputs, cash conversion, capital-provider claims and valuation consistency.

slides.label: 62 Appendix
slides.html:
Reference

Appendix

Core corporate-finance decisions and non-cash expense reminders
slides.note: The remaining slides are optional reference material.

slides.label: 63 Capital budgeting
slides.html:
Appendix · Decision 1

Capital budgeting chooses long-term investments

Reference

Managers identify opportunities whose future cash flows are worth more than the resources required to acquire them.

Invest when value created > cost to acquire

Typical focus: property, plant, equipment, technology, acquisitions, and new products.
slides.note: Link capital budgeting to expected future cash benefits and the required investment.

slides.label: 64 Capital structure
slides.html:
Appendix · Decision 2

Capital structure selects the mix of debt and equity

Reference
Debt

Contractual claim

Interest and repayment commitments can lower flexibility but may reduce the cost of capital.

Equity

Residual ownership

No promised repayment, but investors require compensation for greater risk.

The objective is not “least debt” or “most debt.” It is a financing mix that supports value and resilience.
slides.note: Connect financing choices to flexibility, risk and the cost of capital.

slides.label: 65 Working capital management
slides.html:
Appendix · Decision 3

Working capital management keeps daily operations funded

Reference
Collect

Receivables

Set credit terms and collect cash without sacrificing healthy sales.

Hold

Inventory

Keep enough stock to operate without trapping too much cash.

Pay

Payables

Use supplier credit responsibly while protecting relationships and liquidity.
slides.note: Discuss collections, inventory and supplier terms as operating cash decisions.

slides.label: 66 Capital spending appendix
slides.html:
Appendix · Investing cash flow

Negative investing cash flow can signal deliberate growth

Reference

Capital spending appears in cash flow from investing and includes purchases of long-lived assets.

Large outflows may reflect expansion, new technology, or research and development—not necessarily distress.

Investigate the purpose

Ask what the spending buys

1

Maintenance or growth?

2

Expected return and timing?

3

Funding capacity?
slides.note: Investigate the purpose and expected return of capital spending. Investing cash outflows alone do not establish distress.

slides.label: 67 Depreciation appendix
slides.html:
Appendix · Tangible assets

Depreciation allocates cost; it does not use current-period cash

Reference

Wear, use, and obsolescence reduce a tangible asset’s accounting value over its useful life.

Depreciation is added back in OCF

The original asset purchase was a cash outflow when the asset was acquired.
slides.note: The original asset purchase used cash; this period’s depreciation allocates that cost.

slides.label: 68 Amortization appendix
slides.html:
Appendix · Intangible assets

Amortization spreads an intangible asset’s cost over its useful life

Reference
Patent

Legal protection

Rights to an invention or process.

Trademark

Brand identity

Protected names, symbols, and marks.

Finite-lived IP

Economic benefit

Value consumed over a measurable life.

Amortization is a non-cash expense → add back in OCF
slides.note: Amortization is a noncash allocation; consider whether future replacement spending is required.

</deck-stage>
<script>(function(){
    if(customElements.get('deck-stage'))return;
    class DeckStage extends HTMLElement{
      connectedCallback(){
        if(this._ready)return;
        this._ready=true;
        const W=parseInt(this.getAttribute('width')||1920,10);
        const H=parseInt(this.getAttribute('height')||1080,10);
        this._slides=[...this.querySelectorAll('.slide')];
        this._idx=0;
        try{this._notes=JSON.parse(document.getElementById('speaker-notes')?.textContent||'[]')}catch(error){this._notes=[]}

        const stage=document.createElement('div');
        stage.style.cssText='position:absolute;transform-origin:top left;width:'+W+'px;height:'+H+'px;';
        this._slides.forEach(slide=>{
          slide.style.position='absolute';
          slide.style.top='0';
          slide.style.left='0';
          slide.style.width=W+'px';
          slide.style.height=H+'px';
          slide.style.display='none';
          slide.style.flexDirection='column';
          stage.appendChild(slide);
        });
        this.appendChild(stage);
        this._stage=stage;
        this.style.cssText='display:block;position:fixed;inset:0;width:100vw;height:100vh;overflow:hidden;background:var(--ink);';

        const counter=document.createElement('div');
        counter.setAttribute('aria-live','polite');
        counter.style.cssText='position:fixed;bottom:20px;left:50%;transform:translateX(-50%);background:rgba(0,0,0,.68);color:var(--white);font:500 24px/1 var(--font-mono);padding:10px 18px;border-radius:22px;pointer-events:none;z-index:9999';
        document.body.appendChild(counter);
        this._counter=counter;

        const buttonStyle='position:fixed;bottom:20px;z-index:9999;background:rgba(0,0,0,.64);border:1px solid rgba(255,255,255,.32);color:var(--white);font:600 24px/1 var(--font-body);width:52px;height:52px;border-radius:50%;cursor:pointer;';
        const makeButton=(label,html,right,action)=>{
          const button=document.createElement('button');
          button.type='button';
          button.innerHTML=html;
          button.setAttribute('aria-label',label);
          button.title=label;
          button.style.cssText=buttonStyle+'right:'+right+'px';
          button.addEventListener('click',event=>{event.stopPropagation();action()});
          document.body.appendChild(button);
          return button;
        };
        this._previous=makeButton('Previous slide','←',156,()=>this._go(this._idx-1));
        this._next=makeButton('Next slide','→',92,()=>this._go(this._idx+1));
        this._fullscreen=makeButton('Enter fullscreen','⛶',28,()=>this._toggleFullscreen());

        const notes=document.createElement('div');
        notes.style.cssText='position:fixed;bottom:88px;left:50%;transform:translateX(-50%);max-width:1100px;width:90%;background:rgba(10,10,20,.96);color:var(--white);font:400 24px/1.5 var(--font-body);padding:18px 22px;border-radius:10px;display:none;z-index:9998';
        notes.setAttribute('role','note');
        document.body.appendChild(notes);
        this._notesEl=notes;

        document.addEventListener('keydown',event=>{
          const interactiveTarget=event.target instanceof HTMLElement
            && event.target.closest('input,textarea,select,button,[contenteditable="true"]');
          if(interactiveTarget&&['ArrowRight','ArrowDown',' ','PageDown','ArrowLeft','ArrowUp','PageUp','Home','End'].includes(event.key))return;
          if(['ArrowRight','ArrowDown',' ','PageDown'].includes(event.key)){event.preventDefault();this._go(this._idx+1)}
          if(['ArrowLeft','ArrowUp','PageUp'].includes(event.key)){event.preventDefault();this._go(this._idx-1)}
          if(event.key==='Home'){event.preventDefault();this._go(0)}
          if(event.key==='End'){event.preventDefault();this._go(this._slides.length-1)}
          if(event.key==='n'||event.key==='N')this._toggleNotes();
          if(event.key==='f'||event.key==='F')this._toggleFullscreen();
        });
        this.addEventListener('click',event=>{
          if(event.target.closest('button,a,input,textarea,select,summary'))return;
          const x=event.clientX/window.innerWidth;
          if(x<.33)this._go(this._idx-1);
          else if(x>.67)this._go(this._idx+1);
        });
        window.addEventListener('resize',()=>this._scale());
        window.addEventListener('hashchange',()=>{
          const target=this._indexFromHash();
          if(target!==null&&target!==this._idx)this._go(target,{updateHash:false});
        });
        document.addEventListener('fullscreenchange',()=>this._syncFullscreenButton());

        this._scale();
        this._go(this._indexFromHash()??0,{updateHash:true});
      }
      _indexFromHash(){
        const match=location.hash.match(/^#slide-(\d+)$/);
        if(!match)return null;
        const index=Number(match[1])-1;
        return Number.isInteger(index)&&index>=0&&index<this._slides.length?index:null;
      }
      _scale(){
        const W=parseInt(this.getAttribute('width')||1920,10);
        const H=parseInt(this.getAttribute('height')||1080,10);
        const scale=Math.min(window.innerWidth/W,window.innerHeight/H);
        const offsetX=(window.innerWidth-W*scale)/2;
        const offsetY=(window.innerHeight-H*scale)/2;
        this._stage.style.transform='translate('+offsetX+'px,'+offsetY+'px) scale('+scale+')';
      }
      _go(nextIndex,{updateHash=true}={}){
        const index=Math.max(0,Math.min(nextIndex,this._slides.length-1));
        if(this._slides[this._idx])this._slides[this._idx].style.display='none';
        this._idx=index;
        if(this._slides[index])this._slides[index].style.display='block';
        this._counter.textContent=(index+1)+' / '+this._slides.length;
        this._previous.disabled=index===0;
        this._next.disabled=index===this._slides.length-1;
        this._previous.style.opacity=index===0?'.42':'1';
        this._next.style.opacity=index===this._slides.length-1?'.42':'1';
        if(this._notesEl.style.display==='block')this._notesEl.textContent=this._notes[index]||'No speaker note for this slide.';
        if(updateHash){
          const hash='#slide-'+(index+1);
          if(location.hash!==hash)history.replaceState(null,'',hash);
        }
        this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('slideIndexChanged',{detail:{index,slide:index+1}}));
      }
      _toggleNotes(){
        const opening=this._notesEl.style.display!=='block';
        this._notesEl.style.display=opening?'block':'none';
        if(opening)this._notesEl.textContent=this._notes[this._idx]||'No speaker note for this slide.';
      }
      async _toggleFullscreen(){
        try{
          if(!document.fullscreenElement)await document.documentElement.requestFullscreen();
          else await document.exitFullscreen();
        }catch(error){
          console.warn('Fullscreen is unavailable in this browser context.',error);
        }
      }
      _syncFullscreenButton(){
        const active=Boolean(document.fullscreenElement);
        this._fullscreen.setAttribute('aria-label',active?'Exit fullscreen':'Enter fullscreen');
        this._fullscreen.title=active?'Exit fullscreen':'Enter fullscreen';
      }
    }
    customElements.define('deck-stage',DeckStage);
  })();</script>
